To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
clinically relevant doses (1-5 Gy) of ionizing radiation activate ErbB2, which leads to upregulation of 14- 3-3ζ and FoxM1 and subsequent invasion of breast cancer cell lines.

clinically relevant doses and times of ionizing radiation induce cellular invasion of Erbb2-expressing cancer cells, and that Erbb2, 14-3-zeta and FoxM1 are necessary and/or sufficient for radiation-induced invasion.
ErbB2 activation and 14- 3-3ζ upregulation prime breast cancer cells to invade in response to ionization radiation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which ionizing radiation (X-rays) promotes invasion in breast cancer cells, particularly those expressing high levels of the oncogene ErbB2.
how breast cancer cells become more invasive after exposure to radiation and how we can prevent this process.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the invasion of premalignant breast lesions and how these mechanisms are influenced by radiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ErbB2, Foxm1, and 14- 3-3ζ are key mediators in radiation-induced breast cancer cell invasion.
ErbB2, 14-3-zeta and FoxM1 collaborate to prime breast cancer cells to invasion in response to IR.
ErbB2, Foxm1 and 14.3.3ζ are all required to prime breast cancer cells to invasion in response to IR.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ionizing radiation (X-rays) activates the ErbB2 receptor tyrosine kinase in breast cancer cells.

ionizing radiation (X-rays) activates the epidermal growth-factor receptor (ErbB2) in breast cancer cells, which leads to upregulation of FoxM1 transcription factor, its target gene, MMP2, and the scaffold protein 14-3ζ.
ionizing radiation activates ErbB2, which then activates 14-3-zeta, which in turn activates FoxM1, which promotes invasion of breast cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ErbB2 expression in breast cancer cells is sufficient to render them sensitive to radiation-induced invasion.

ErbB2, Foxm1, and 14- 3-3ζ contribute to the invasive phenotype of breast cancer cells following exposure to clinically relevant doses of radiation, and that inhibition of these proteins may enhance the efficacy of radiation therapy.
ErbB2 signaling and the downstream transcription factor, Foxm1, are important for invasion in response radiation.
